issues.failure_explanation: The abstract and conclusion assert that theoretical error bounds are derived for both proposed approaches (Algorithms 1 and 2). The only bounds in the paper are Theorem 3.4 (a pure existence statement about some rank-R factorization) and Corollary 4.2 (which requires the selected core to have maximal volume among all S_1×S_2 submatrices). Algorithms 1 and 2 select fixed nested symmetric index intervals around frequency 0 with a heuristic σ_min-based stopping rule; nothing shows their core has maximal volume, and no error bound relating τ, (b_1,b_2) or the output to ‖f−F̃f‖ is proved. The advertised 'rigorous control over approximation quality' for the algorithms is therefore unsupported.

failure_location.quote: Theoretical error bounds are derived for both approaches, ensuring rigorous control over approximation quality.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the abstract, Section 4.2 and conclusion to say that error bounds are given only for an idealized (maximal-volume) selection and for existence of a low-rank factorization, and that the adaptive algorithms are heuristics without a proven error guarantee; or add a genuine analysis of the algorithms' output.
issues.overall_effect: The claimed guarantees for the actual computational methods (Algorithms 1, 2, and the appendix variant) are unsupported; only existence/idealized-selection bounds are available.
issues.title: Prose claims error bounds for the adaptive algorithms, but none is derived for them
issues.why_classification: Correcting the claim withdraws the advertised guarantee for the algorithms but the remaining formal results and methods are unchanged; a genuine bound would require a new nontrivial argument.

issues.failure_explanation: With the normalized inner product, Parseval gives ‖F̃f−Ff‖_{L^2} = ‖A−EF*‖_F exactly. The Frobenius norm dominates the max-entry norm, ‖·‖_F ≥ ‖·‖_max, and can exceed it by a factor √((2I_1+1)(2I_2+1)) (e.g. when all entries of A−EF* have equal modulus). So the asserted inequality ‖F̃f−Ff‖_{L^2} ≤ ‖A−EF*‖_max is false in general, and Theorem 3.3's max-norm bound εʼ‖A‖_2 cannot be transferred to the L2 error. Converting properly would require ε‖A‖_2√((2I_1+1)(2I_2+1)), or a rank of order (2I_1+1)(2I_2+1)ln(·)/ε², which is vacuous. Corollary 4.2 uses the same false transfer from Theorem 4.1's max-norm bound.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must replace the max-norm ε-rank input by a Frobenius-norm (or spectral) low-rank error bound and restate the theorem and corollary with the resulting rank/error trade-off, which loses the dimension-free logarithmic rank claim.
issues.overall_effect: The central theoretical guarantee that a rank R = O(ln(I_1+I_2)/ε²) approximation achieves L2 error ε‖A‖_2 (Theorem 3.4), and the corresponding CUR bound in Corollary 4.2, are unproven and, as stated, false in general.
issues.title: L2 error bounded by max-entry norm: Frobenius/Parseval identity contradicts the key inequality
issues.why_classification: The logarithmic-rank L2 guarantee, the main theoretical result of Section 3, does not survive any repair supported by the source; the corollary in Section 4 fails for the same reason.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof bounds ‖Ff−f‖_{L^2} by invoking Theorem 3.1, which yields C min{I_1,I_2}^{-α}|f|_α. The statement instead claims C max{I_1,I_2}^{-α}|f|_α, which is strictly smaller when I_1≠I_2 and is not implied (a function with energy at frequencies k_1 ≈ min{I_1,I_2} but |k_2| ≤ I_2 large shows the max-version fails). Corollary 4.2 repeats the same overstated term.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace max{I_1,I_2} by min{I_1,I_2} in both statements.
issues.overall_effect: The truncation term in Theorem 3.4 and Corollary 4.2 is overstated for anisotropic truncation orders.
issues.title: Truncation term stated with max{I_1,I_2} although Theorem 3.1 only gives min{I_1,I_2}
issues.why_classification: A local restatement matching the invoked theorem fixes it; only the sharpness for I_1≠I_2 is withdrawn.

issues.failure_explanation: Section 4.2.1 defines termination when the maximum of the two normalized σ_min ratios drops below τ (both C and R numerically rank-deficient), whereas Algorithm 1 sets tol to the minimum of the ratios and stops when tol ≤ τ (either one rank-deficient). These are different rules that produce different index sets S_1,S_2 and different outputs; the procedure is not uniquely specified and the two descriptions cannot both be the intended method.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Choose one criterion (max or min) and make the prose and pseudocode agree.
issues.overall_effect: The output and integral count of Algorithm 1 (and the numerical comparisons using it) depend on which rule is meant.
issues.title: Algorithm 1 stopping rule: prose (max, both small) and pseudocode (min, one small) disagree
issues.why_classification: Either choice yields a well-defined heuristic with the same structure; the fix is a local edit with no loss of proven content.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we need to obtain three matrices $\mathbf{G}_{1k}\in\mathbb{C}^{(2(k-1)b_1+1)\times 2b_2}$, $\mathbf{G}_{2k}\in\mathbb{C}^{2b_1\times (2(k-1)b_2+1)}$

issues.failure_explanation: In Algorithms 1, 2 and C.1, k is initialized to 0 and incremented only after the selection step, so the first pass uses k=0, giving T_n' = [0:b_n−1] ∪ [−b_n+1:0] = [−b_n+1:b_n−1], which contains 0 already in T_n and has 2b_n−1 (not 2b_n) elements. In Algorithm 1 this appends a duplicate of the existing column/row for frequency 0, forcing σ_min(C)=σ_min(R)=0 and tol=0 ≤ τ immediately; in Algorithms 2 and C.1 the block sizes stated (2(k−1)b_n+1 and 2b_n) and the counts S_n=2Kb_n+1 no longer match, and G acquires duplicated rows/columns making G singular. As written, the procedures do not perform the intended index expansion.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Start the iteration counter at k=1 (or increment k before selecting T_n') so that T_n' = [−kb_n:−(k−1)b_n−1] ∪ [(k−1)b_n+1:kb_n] is disjoint from T_n.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithms 1, 2 and C.1 as written are degenerate on the first iteration; the stated sizes S_n=2Kb_n+1 and block dimensions do not match the pseudocode.
issues.title: Off-by-one loop index: first iteration re-selects index 0, producing duplicated columns and degenerate σ_min
issues.why_classification: A one-line index correction restores the intended procedure and all stated sizes, with no loss of content.

Compute $\mathbf{C}$ according to (\ref{t-lasso:method-one:sub1-main}) with $\mathbb{T}_2$, and $\mathbf{R}$ according to (\ref{t-lasso:method-one:sub2-main}) with $\mathbb{T}_1$.
it requires $(2I_1+1)S_2+(2I_2+1)S_1-S_1S_2$ multiple integrals to form the pair $\{\mathbf{C},\mathbf{R}\}$

issues.failure_explanation: Algorithm C.1 still computes the full matrices C ∈ C^{(2I_1+1)×S_2} and R ∈ C^{S_1×(2I_2+1)}, which are needed in full for C G^† R. The set of distinct coefficients in C ∪ R has exactly (2I_1+1)S_2+(2I_2+1)S_1−S_1S_2 entries, so this many double integrals are required regardless of how G is assembled; the diagonal blocks G_k are themselves entries of C. The stated count subtracts 2S_1S_2 (double-counting the overlap) and adds Kb_1b_2 (the diagonal blocks actually total 1+4Kb_1b_2), and is smaller than the number of distinct integrals needed, so it is false; the claim that Algorithm C.1 needs fewer integrals than Algorithms 1 and 2 is therefore unsupported and false. Zeroing the off-diagonal blocks only avoids computing entries that C and R supply anyway, while making G ≠ A(I_1,I_2) so the output is no longer a skeleton approximation.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the count to (2I_1+1)S_2+(2I_2+1)S_1−S_1S_2 and withdraw the claim of fewer integrals, presenting Algorithm C.1 only as reducing the arithmetic cost of σ_min(G) and G^†.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised advantage of the appendix variant (fewer double integrals) does not exist; its integral cost equals that of Algorithms 1 and 2, and its output loses the CUR/cross interpretation.
issues.title: Appendix Algorithm C.1 integral count is wrong; it uses no fewer double integrals than Algorithm 2
issues.why_classification: The algorithm remains well defined and its arithmetic-cost claims survive, but the primary advertised benefit (fewer integrals) must be abandoned and cannot be recovered.
